title: Chapter 16 — That Excessive Care Of Worldly Welfare May Impair That Welfare
paragraphs: There is a closer tie than is commonly supposed between the improvement of the soul and the improvement of what belongs to the body. A man may hold the two apart and consider each in turn, but he cannot separate them completely without finally losing sight of both. The beasts have the same senses we do, and very nearly the same appetites. We have no sensual passions that are not shared with our species and theirs, and that are not found, at least in germ, in a dog as well as in a man. Why then can the animals provide only for their first and lowest needs, while we can endlessly vary and endlessly expand our enjoyments?

We are superior to the beasts in this: we use our souls to discover those material goods toward which they are drawn only by instinct. In man, the angel teaches the brute the art of satisfying its desires. It is because man is capable of rising above the things of the body, and of despising life itself — of which the beasts have not the least notion — that he can multiply those very bodily goods to a degree inferior species are equally incapable of conceiving. Whatever raises, enlarges, and expands the soul makes it more capable of succeeding even in undertakings that do not concern it. Whatever, on the other hand, weakens or debases it makes it weaker for all purposes, the greatest as well as the least, and threatens to render it almost equally powerless in both. That is why the soul must remain great and strong, even if only to devote that strength and greatness from time to time to the service of the body. If men were ever to content themselves with material objects, they would probably lose by degrees the art of producing them, and would end up enjoying them like the brutes — without discernment and without improvement.
